title: Lesson 1: Constitutional Foundations
subtitle: The Biblical and Historical Roots of the Constitution
primary_source: The Preamble to the United States Constitution (1787)
key_concepts: Biblical basis for separation of powers

verses.text: "For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; it is he who will save us."
verses.commentary: This single verse describes three functions of government — judicial, legislative, and executive — all united in God. The Founders recognized that since only God can be trusted with all three powers, human government must divide them among separate branches to prevent tyranny.

verses.text: "The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?"
verses.commentary: The Founders understood the Biblical doctrine of human sinfulness. Because all people are fallen, no individual or group can be trusted with unlimited power. The Constitution's system of checks and balances reflects this sober Biblical realism.

content.heading: Introduction: A Government Like No Other
paragraphs: When the delegates gathered in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787, they set out to create something extraordinary: a government powerful enough to maintain order but limited enough to protect liberty. The Constitution they produced has endured for over two centuries, making it the oldest written national constitution still in use.

The Constitution was not designed in a vacuum. Its principles were drawn from Biblical teaching, English common law, and the hard lessons of history. Understanding these foundations is essential to understanding how our government works and why it was designed the way it was.

content.heading: Biblical Principles in the Constitution
paragraphs: The Founders were deeply influenced by the Bible, even those who were not orthodox Christians. Several key Constitutional principles have clear Biblical roots.

The separation of powers reflects Isaiah 33:22, which attributes judicial, legislative, and executive authority to God alone. Since no human being is God, no human being should hold all three powers. James Madison wrote in Federalist No. 51: 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary' — a clear echo of the Biblical doctrine of sin.

The rule of law — the idea that the law applies equally to everyone, including rulers — comes from Deuteronomy 17:18-20, where even the king of Israel was required to read and obey God's law. No one is above the law because all are accountable to God.

The concept of individual rights — life, liberty, and property — flows from the Biblical teaching that every person is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27) and therefore possesses inherent dignity and worth.

content.heading: The Structure of the Constitution
paragraphs: The Constitution establishes a federal republic — a system in which power is divided between a national government and state governments, and citizens elect representatives to govern on their behalf.

The document is organized into seven Articles. Article I establishes the Legislative Branch (Congress), Article II the Executive Branch (the President), and Article III the Judicial Branch (the courts). The remaining articles address federalism, the amendment process, the supremacy of the Constitution, and ratification.

The first ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791 to explicitly protect individual liberties such as freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly, and the right to bear arms. These rights are understood not as grants from government but as God-given rights that government must protect.

content.heading: Why the Constitution Matters Today
paragraphs: The Constitution matters because it limits government power and protects individual liberty. Without it, there would be no legal barrier to prevent the government from taking away your freedoms.

As citizens, we have a duty to understand the Constitution, defend its principles, and hold our leaders accountable to its provisions. The Founders knew that self-government requires an informed and virtuous citizenry. As Benjamin Franklin reportedly said when asked what kind of government the Convention had created: 'A republic, if you can keep it.'

reflection_questions.question: How does Isaiah 33:22 relate to the structure of the U.S. government? Why did the Founders divide governmental power into three branches?
reflection_questions.guidance: Consider why concentrating all power in one person or group is dangerous. Think about how the Biblical understanding of human sinfulness informed the Founders' design.

reflection_questions.question: What does it mean that the Constitution establishes a 'republic' rather than a pure democracy? Why did the Founders choose this form of government?
reflection_questions.guidance: Think about the difference between direct democracy (majority rule) and a republic (rule of law through elected representatives). Consider the Founders' concern about 'the tyranny of the majority.'

reflection_questions.question: Why is it important for citizens to understand the Constitution? What happens to liberty when citizens are ignorant of their rights and their government's limits?
reflection_questions.guidance: Consider Franklin's warning about keeping the republic. Think about specific ways an informed citizenry protects liberty.
